topic: MVI: intents, reducers & single immutable state

questions.question: In MVI, what does a reducer do?
options: Takes current state and an intent or result, returns a new state, with no side effects
Collects the repository's flows and caches their latest values for the rest of the screen
Renders the current state into composables and sends the user's clicks to the ViewModel
Routes each incoming intent to whichever of several ViewModels is able to handle it
questions.explanation: A reducer is a pure function `(State, Intent or Result) -> State`. Because it only computes a new state from its inputs, it is deterministic and easy to unit test. Data loading and rendering live elsewhere: in the ViewModel's effect handling and in the UI.

questions.question: In MVI the UI state is typically an immutable data class, and changes are made by creating a new instance with `copy()` instead of mutating fields.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Immutable state means every change produces a new value that can be compared, logged or replayed, and the UI can never see a half-modified object. It also plays well with StateFlow, which only emits when the new value is not equal to the old one.

questions.question: Compared with exposing `isLoading`, `items` and `error` as three separate StateFlows, what does one `StateFlow<UiState>` give you? Select all that apply.
options: All fields change together, so the UI never renders a half-updated mix
A single place to see and log exactly what the screen is showing
Automatic restore of the screen after the process has been killed
Fewer recompositions in every case, whatever the UI reads
questions.explanation: With one state object, an update such as loading false plus items set is a single emission, so there is no moment where both a spinner and the error show. It also gives a single source of truth to debug or snapshot in tests. It does not persist anything, and reading one large object at the top of the UI can even cause more recomposition, not less.

questions.question: What is wrong with this reducer?
options: It performs a side effect, so the reducer is no longer pure or safely repeatable
copy() inside a when branch creates a new state object that the StateFlow never emits
A reducer has to be a suspend function, so the call to refresh() needs to be awaited
isLoading should be updated only once the refresh has finished, not before calling it
questions.explanation: Starting the refresh inside the reducer makes it impure: testing or replaying it triggers network calls. In MVI the reducer only returns the new state, and the ViewModel or an effect handler starts the work and later reports the outcome as another intent or result. Setting `isLoading = true` up front is correct.

questions.question: Why model intents as a `sealed interface` and handle them in a `when` with no `else` branch?
options: Adding a new intent makes that when a compile error until the new case is handled
Sealed types dispatch faster at runtime than open classes or plain interfaces do
Sealed intents can be serialized automatically, so they can be logged or replayed
It lets other modules add their own intents without changing the screen's code
questions.explanation: A `when` over a sealed type must be exhaustive, so the compiler points to every place that needs to handle a newly added intent. An `else` branch would hide that. Sealed hierarchies are closed to other modules by design, and they bring no runtime speed-up or serialization of their own.

questions.question: Which are real costs or risks of MVI? Select all that apply.
options: More boilerplate: intent, state and effect types for every screen
Passing one large state through the UI can widen recomposition
Each change allocates a new state object (usually negligible)
It cannot be combined with Jetpack Compose at all
It forbids using coroutines inside the ViewModel
questions.explanation: MVI's costs are ceremony and some care with how the big state is passed down: reading the whole object high in the tree and passing it to every child makes more of the tree depend on each change. Copying data classes allocates, but that is rarely measurable. Compose and coroutines are a natural fit for MVI, not a conflict.

questions.question: Intents are consumed by a single coroutine like this, and `handle` makes suspending network calls. What is the consequence?
options: A slow call delays every later intent, including a Cancel tap, until it has finished
Intents are processed in parallel, so several updates to the state can race each other
An UNLIMITED channel starts dropping intents once a large number of them is queued
The channel conflates intents sent close together, so only the latest one is handled
questions.explanation: A single consumer processes intents strictly in order, which avoids races but means a long `handle` call blocks the queue. Long-running work should be launched separately, with its outcome fed back as a result, so new intents keep flowing. An UNLIMITED channel never drops or conflates elements.

questions.question: Many MVI setups separate Intent (what the user did) from Result or Mutation (what happened). Why?
options: One intent's async work can yield several results over time; the reducer stays pure
Results can be serialized for logging, while intents can't be serialized by Kotlin at all
Reducers may only accept sealed classes that were declared in the data layer of the app
Compose needs the extra type in order to skip recomposition of screens that haven't changed
questions.explanation: One intent such as Refresh can lead to Loading, then Success or Failure, arriving at different times from asynchronous work. Turning each outcome into a result lets the reducer remain a simple, synchronous `(State, Result) -> State`. The split is about modeling and testability, not serialization or Compose.

questions.question: A pure MVI reducer can be unit-tested with plain JUnit calls, without a coroutine test dispatcher, fakes for the repository, or Android dependencies.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A pure reducer is just a function from (state, intent or result) to a new state, so a test calls it with inputs and asserts on the returned state. Coroutines, repositories and dispatchers only come in when testing the effect-handling part of the ViewModel. This cheap testability is one of the main arguments for keeping reducers free of side effects.

questions.question: An MVI screen keeps its whole UiState in a StateFlow. How should it handle process death?
options: Save minimal inputs like query or selected id in SavedStateHandle and reload the rest
Make the whole UiState Parcelable and write all of it into the saved state after every change
Nothing is needed: StateFlow keeps its latest value around after the process has been killed
Store the latest UiState in a companion object so that it can be read back after a restart
questions.explanation: Saved instance state goes through a Bundle with a tight size limit; saving a whole state with lists can cause `TransactionTooLargeException` and slows every save. Persist only what cannot be re-derived (user input, ids, selected tab) and rebuild the rest from the repository. In-memory objects, including companion objects, are gone with the process.
